newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS - U.S. Treasuries poised to fight back.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS - U.S. Treasuries poised to fight back.

text.p: Investors in U.S. Treasuries have had a miserable year so far.
Worries that growth was spiralling out of control, and that inflation would follow, have driven bond buyers out of the U.S. and into Europe's lower-inflation markets such as German Bunds.
But the year is not over.
Now, even as U.S. inflation threatens to perk up, Treasuries look set to outperform their rivals, analysts said on Wednesday.
"Taking a three- to six-month view, U.S. bonds look relatively attractive," said fund manager Paul Meader.

Investors currently demand a 66 basis point yield premium in 10-year U.S. Treasuries compared to German Bunds. The 10-year U.S. T-note at 1240 GMT was yielding 6.53 percent, while Bund yields have fallen below six percent.
Meader, who manages 200 million stg in Guernsey for Matheson Investment Management, said that spread could fall to zero by the end of the first quarter 1997.

By the time the U.S. gets around to tightening monetary policy to prevent inflation from charging higher, markets will have already priced in higher rates. Meanwhile a revival in the German economy could catch investors off guard.
"The risk in the German economy at the moment is that it surprises us with stronger rather than weaker growth," Meader said.
The Treasury turnaround, however, is contingent on U.S. economic developments and the idea that the Federal Reserve has been right in expecting a second-half slowdown.

"If we have a U.S. slowdown and people believe we are going to see a softer economy in the U.S., we will see the bond market react quite positively," said Kim Thomsen, head of fixed income at Danske Invest in Copenhagen, Denmark's largest investment fund with $2.0 billion.
Thomsen said that in that case the U.S./German yield spread could narrow to 35 basis points by year-end.
Eagerly awaited consumer price figures on Wednesday showed year-on-year growth of three percent in September. By comparison, latest German data showed 1.4 percent inflation.

"Yes U.S. CPI is higher than Germany's and it will probably tick higher rather than lower over the course of the next six months to a year," said Meader. But, rightly or wrongly, markets were more focused on growth which was expected to fall.
Adrian Schmidt, international economist at Chase in London, echoed that view. "In general people are taking a relatively relaxed approach to inflation," he said.
"People generally think the economy is slowing down and even if there are a few blips there doesn't seem to be the underlying pressure to cause a pickup in inflation."

Thomsen said Treasuries have such a domestic focus that inflation comparisons to countries such as Germany did not sway investors much. "An investor in Dallas doesn't care what the real yield is in Germany," he said.
Capital flows also could turn in Treasuries' favour, analysts said.

Japanese funds have been seeping out of Japan, noticeably into Europe, while at the same time European convergence trades have been the dominant theme in recent months on the expectation of a smooth path to European economic and monetary union (EMU).
"If you have any qualms about EMU... then you will see Japan start to divert their flow of funds away from Europe and toward the U.S.," he said.
Schmidt at Chase said the yield premium in Treasuries was attractive to prevent further Bund outperformance but he doubted there was scope for a move back parity between the two.
